name: tutorial_say_versus_do
document:
# Tutorial: Say versus Do

## Purpose

An organisation says one thing in public and asks government for another. Reporting in
this genre is the two texts read together: the lead is not an advocacy record on its own,
it is a record that asks for something its own promise cannot easily be squared with.
This workflow puts each promise beside the ask, has a model propose how the two stand,
sends every proposed contradiction to a person, and publishes what that person decided.

The six records here are real, and every one of them is hard. A reader cannot tell the
answer from the two sentences without thinking: two of the six are contradictions at the
level of the mechanism rather than the goal, one reads exactly like a contradiction and
is not, two are genuinely arguable, and one is an organisation lobbying for the rule it
already meets. That is the point of the sample — a set of obvious cases would teach the
reader nothing about the judgement they are being asked to check.

## Where this data came from

Each record was assembled by hand from two published pages: one where the organisation
states its commitment, one where it states what it asked government for. Both pages are
linked from every row of the report, and the full provenance — the quoted line each
sentence was written from, both links, both dates, whether the page is the organisation's
own or an outlet's account of it, and the reasoning behind the label a researcher gave
the pair — is bundled beside this workflow as
`app/seeds/data/sources/tutorial_say_versus_do.json`.

Two things this sample does NOT carry, because the sources do not: no lobbying firm, and
no money. There is no spend column, no filing id and no registrant, because none of these
records is a lobbying disclosure. Anything of that kind on this page would have been
invented, and an invented figure beside a real organisation's name is the exact failure
this tool exists to prevent.

Dates are recorded as the source states them. Several of these pages carry no publication
date at all, so their date field reads `undated policy page (fetched 2026-08-13)` rather
than a date nobody published. That is uglier than a clean date column and it is the
honest shape of the data.

## Input data

Two bundled CSVs.

`tutorial_lobbying_records.csv`, one row per advocacy record:

- `record_id` — the research set's own case id, unique
- `organisation` — who made the ask
- `period` — the stretch the two sources span, e.g. "2023-2024"
- `lobbying_issue` — one sentence on what this organisation asked government for
- `lobbying_quote` — the line from the source that sentence was written from
- `lobbying_source_url` — the page it was read on
- `lobbying_source_date` — what that page says about its own date

`tutorial_public_commitments.csv`, one row per organisation:

- `organisation` — who made the commitment
- `public_commitment` — one sentence on what it said in public it would do
- `commitment_quote` — the line from the source that sentence was written from
- `commitment_source_url` — the page it was read on
- `commitment_source_date` — what that page says about its own date

Both files declare every column as required, so a blank commitment, a blank promise or a
missing link fails the step that reads the file rather than travelling on as an empty
cell.

## Step 1 — Refuse a claim with no source

Every advocacy record is read before anything else touches it, and the run stops on one
that cannot be checked: a source link that is absent or is not an http or https address,
an empty account of what was asked for, or a source that says nothing about when it was
published or read. The link that survives is carried forward trimmed of surrounding
space. A claim with no source does not enter this workflow, because a claim nobody can
open is a claim nobody can check — and every row of the published report is an invitation
to check it. This is plain code, not the model: whether a link is a link has one right
answer.

## Step 2 — Put each promise beside the ask

Bring `public_commitment`, `commitment_quote`, `commitment_source_url` and
`commitment_source_date` onto every advocacy record, matched on the organisation's name.
The commitments file carries at most one row per organisation, and a repeat would fail
the run rather than quietly multiplying records. No record is dropped here. A record for
an organisation with no commitment row keeps every one of its own fields and carries a
blank commitment — the absence is the record, and the next step is told to read it as an
absence rather than as a judgment.

## Step 3 — Judge the ask against the promise (LLM)

For each record, read the organisation's public commitment and this record's ask
together, and add two fields — one record in, one record out (the record is neither
dropped nor duplicated):

- `ai_judgment` — one of: Contradicts, Matches, Unclear, No commitment given.
  "Contradicts" means the ask cannot be squared with the promise. "No commitment given"
  is the answer when the commitment field is blank. Every record gets one of the four and
  none is left blank: the absent-commitment case already has its own label, so a blank
  would be a hole in what the report later prints rather than an answer.
- `ai_justification` — a single plain sentence naming what the organisation said and what
  it asked for.

The organisations are real, which makes the instruction stricter rather than looser: the
model is told to judge only the two texts printed in front of it, because what it half
remembers about a real company or trade association is not evidence, is not on this
record, and cannot be checked by the person who reads its answer. It is told not to
invent, complete or paraphrase a commitment that is not printed. The step names the model
it runs on, so the run records which model answered rather than whichever one the
platform happened to default to that week.

Records are read up to twelve at a time in one model call — up to, because the last call
of a run holds whatever is left over. All six of these travel in a single call. This is a
cost trade: one call carrying twelve records is far cheaper than twelve calls carrying
one. What it costs is independence, since the records sharing a call are judged beside
each other, so a record's answer could be swayed by the ones it happens to travel with.

## Step 4 — Put every contradiction in front of a person

A contradiction is the one judgment this workflow publishes as a finding, so the model's
is not the one that gets published. Every record the model called "Contradicts" is queued
for a human, and the run stops there — nothing below this step runs until each queued
record has been decided.

The card is deliberately narrow. The reviewer is shown the record's id, the organisation,
the promise, the ask, the model's label and the model's sentence — and nothing else,
because everything else is furniture to a decision made from two texts. They record a
label of their own in `reviewed_judgment`. The model's `ai_judgment` is left exactly as
the model wrote it, so what the model said and what the person decided are both on the
record afterwards. Beside their label the reviewer records the name they reviewed under,
the moment they decided, and a note naming the words in the two texts they decided from.

This step decides nothing itself. A queued record with no recorded decision stays queued
and the run stays stopped: there is no wait that expires and no label that stands in for
one nobody chose. A record the model did not call a contradiction is not queued, is read
by nobody, and passes through unchanged.

After this step every record carries `review_verdict`: "approve" where the reviewer kept
the model's label, "modify" where they changed it, and "skipped" for a record no person
was asked about — so a judgment a person reviewed can be told from one only the model
made.

## Step 5 — Publish the report

Produce a single HTML page listing every record with the organisation, the period, what
it said in public, what it asked government for, and the judgment as it stands after
review. Both texts carry a link to the page they were read on, because the link is the
point: a reader who does not believe a row can open both sides of it and decide for
themselves.

The label the page prints is the reviewer's, not the model's: a record whose reviewer
changed the label is no longer printed as a contradiction, and a contradiction they
confirmed carries their name, the time they reviewed it and the note they left. A
judgment recorded as reviewed with nobody's name against it is not published at all: the
step stops instead. No score, no ranking and no recommendation: the report is a reading
aid, not a verdict, and it makes no accusation of its own — it shows two sourced texts
and says which person decided how they stand.

Every row also carries a link back to that row's lineage — each stage that touched it,
back to the input row it came from — so a reader can check any line of the page against
the run.

The page's markup and stylesheet live in the step that writes them, so a reviewer reads
the markup and the code that fills it together.

## Out of scope

No external fetching, no record dropped anywhere, and nothing matched twice — one check,
one match, one model read, one human review, one page.

stages.description: Judge the Ask Against the Public Commitment
compiler_notes: Grain is strictly 1:1 — the document states no record is dropped or duplicated here.

public_commitment is nullable because the match leaves it blank for an organisation with no commitment row; the prompt names that case and fixes its answer to 'No commitment given', so an absence is never read as a judgment.
The organisations are real, so the prompt forbids using anything the model knows about them: an answer resting on what a model half remembers is one the reader cannot check against either source.
The model is shown the quoted line beside each paraphrase, so its judgment rests on the source's own words rather than only on the sentence a researcher wrote from them.

batch_size 12 amortises the instructions prefix across up to twelve records per call, and each call is a process spawn, so the batch size sets how long a run takes; the six bundled records are one call. The records in a call share one context, which the document accepts and states as the cost of the saving.

adds.description: How this ask stands against the organisation's public commitment; one of the four labels on every record.

adds.name: ai_justification
adds.description: One sentence naming what the organisation said in public and what it asked government for.

source.section: Step 3 — Judge the ask against the promise (LLM)

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are reading one thing an organisation asked government for against what the same organisation has said in public.

Return a JSON object with exactly these two fields:

1. "ai_judgment": exactly one of — Contradicts | Matches | Unclear | No commitment given
   - "Contradicts": the ask cannot be squared with the commitment.
   - "Matches": the ask asks government for what the commitment says.
   - "Unclear": the two texts are about different things, or neither supports nor conflicts with the other.
   - "No commitment given": the commitment line is blank, or reads `nan` or `None` because no commitment was on record for that organisation. Answer this and nothing else in that case — do not judge, and do not supply a commitment yourself.

2. "ai_justification": one plain sentence naming what the organisation said in public and what it asked government for. Empty string when there is no commitment to compare against.

These are real organisations, which makes this rule stricter, not looser: judge ONLY the two texts printed below. What you know or think you remember about this organisation is not evidence, is not on this record, and cannot be checked by the person who reads your answer — so a judgment resting on it is one nobody can defend. Never invent, complete or paraphrase a commitment that is not printed here.

Worked example — the case most easily got wrong, an organisation with no commitment on record. Given:

  Organisation: Example Bakery Group
  What it said in public: nan
  In the source's words: "nan"
  What it asked government for: The group asked Parliament to make country-of-origin labelling compulsory for every baker.
  In the source's words: "a level playing field on origin labelling"

  {"ai_judgment": "No commitment given", "ai_justification": ""}

Nothing was said in public there, so there is nothing to judge the ask against, and supplying a commitment of your own would be inventing the evidence.

stages.description: Put Every Contradiction in Front of a Person
compiler_notes: queue.filter selects only the records the model called 'Contradicts': those are the only ones the report prints as a finding, so queueing the other three labels would spend a reviewer's attention on rows nothing is claimed about.

The reviewer sees exactly the columns the signature reads, so this signature reads the six the decision is made from and nothing else — the quotes, the links and the dates are on the report, not on the card.
No queue.sort: a sort key has to be read, so ordering the queue would put a column back on the card that the decision is not made from.

The reviewer's label is ADDED as reviewed_judgment; the model's ai_judgment is never overwritten, so the run records both what the model said and what the person decided, and the report can print the second beside the first.

reviewed_judgment is non-nullable: a queued row's reviewer picks one of the four labels, and a row the filter passed over carries the model's label through unchanged, so no record reaches the report unlabelled.

adds.name: reviewed_judgment
adds.description: How this ask stands against the commitment, as the reviewer left it; the model's own answer stays in `ai_judgment`.

adds.name: review_verdict
adds.description: 'approve' where the reviewer kept the model's label, 'modify' where they changed it, 'skipped' for a record no person was asked about.

adds.name: reviewer
adds.description: The name the reviewer decided under; null on a record no person was asked about.

adds.name: reviewed_at
adds.description: When the reviewer recorded that decision; null on a record no person was asked about.

source.section: Step 4 — Put every contradiction in front of a person

queue.reviewer_instructions: You are the last reader before this record is published as a contradiction, and the report will carry your name against it. Read the promise and the ask, and decide from those two texts — the model's label is a proposal, and agreeing with one you have not checked is how a wrong finding gets published under your name. These are real organisations, so what you already believe about this one is not evidence either. Keep 'Contradicts' only if the ask cannot be squared with the promise; if the two are about different things, or the ask asks for what was promised, change the label to the one that fits. Then say in the note which words in the two texts you decided from.

compiler_notes: Both texts are printed with a link to the page they were read on: the link is what makes a row checkable, and a row nobody can check is the thing this workflow exists against.
The document says this is a reading aid, not a verdict — no score, ranking or recommendation column is rendered, and the page states that the judgement is a person's, not the tool's.

What is printed is reviewed_judgment, the label as the reviewer left it. The model's ai_judgment is read too, but only to say what a reviewer changed it FROM — nothing on this page claims a contradiction the model alone asserted.
A record published as contradicting a commitment nothing matched stops the step: the page must not show a contradiction it cannot print both sides of.
A commitment with no link stops the step too: printing one would be a claim the reader cannot check.
The page's markup lives in this step, beside the code that fills it, so a reviewer reads both together rather than chasing a file the workflow does not carry.
This stage writes the HTML to disk and returns a file-path pointer rather than embedding the markup inline, which is practical at scale.

function.summary: Fills the committed report template — one row per record, in the order they arrived — with the promise and the ask, each linked to the page it was read on, and the judgment as the reviewer left it.
